_note: Floors for scripts/check_evals.sh, measured on mlx-community/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-4bit on 2026-08-15. Each floor is the measured score minus one iteration's worth of slack, because every suite samples only 5 iterations per case and a single flaky iteration is normal — the actor suite scored 100.0% and then 95.0% back to back with no code change between them. A real regression moves more than one run and still trips these. Re-measure and edit deliberately when a change legitimately moves a number; never lower one just to get green.

coach._measured: 87.4% Japanese mean (2026-09-06) after the たくさん example was made one-directional and the particle rule scoped to sentence-final particles; the Japanese arm read 87.0 / 87.8 / 87.0 / 87.0 / 87.4 across five runs against 83.0, and every edit in that change applies only to Japanese. Headline over the same six runs: 84.2 / 84.2 / 87.9 / 87.3 / 84.5 / 86.7. Floor raised 65.0 -> 80.0, which is 4.2 points under the LOWEST of those six, not under the mean — the headline is the noisier number because the English situational fixtures swing on identical code (case 58 "Give me a large coffee." read 0/5, 5/5, 4/5 and 2/5 across runs, and the English arm moved 10 points with no English-affecting change in the tree). 80.0 is deliberately conservative for that reason: this repo has twice set an actor floor from too few runs and had the next reading trip it, and a floor that fires on noise trains people to ignore it. Anything above 82 would sit inside the observed English swing. 84.2% (278/330) on 2026-09-05 after the five Japanese coach nets; 70.0% (231/330) after level-up fit promotion (2026-09-04); 68.2% (225/330) after the transitivity and counter nets (2026-09-02); was 60.6% (200/330) honest headline on 2026-08-29, 72 cases x 5 with 6 prompt-example cases excluded; 63.9% (230/360) including them. One run of slack = 0.30 points. Floor raised 59.0 -> 65.0, which is 3.2 points under the measured value: the same 52-case set once read 59.6% then 60.9% with no code change, so real drift here is around 1.3 points, and 65.0 leaves more than twice that. The gain is deterministic, not model luck — apply_transitivity_net and apply_counter_net take six cases from 0-1/5 to 5/5 in code — so unlike a prompt-driven gain it should not decay.
coach._measured_history: Was 59.6% (137/230) against 52 cases. 20 situational-appropriateness cases were added on 2026-08-29 (12 violations, 8 appropriate counterexamples, both languages), so the ruler is now 72 cases. Like the 2026-08-15 expansion, the number moved because the ruler changed, not the coach: the same 52 cases scored 140/230 before the feature and 141/230 after it.
coach._why_the_headline_excludes_six: Cases 5, 6, 7, 8, 11 and 12 are quoted verbatim in COACH_SYS, so the prompt hands the model the answer and they cannot fail. Proven, not assumed: those six scored 30/30 while six new cases testing the SAME rules with novel sentences scored 22/30. The sharpest pair is plural-after-a-number — 'two bottle' (in the prompt) 5/5 against 'four ticket' (novel) 2/5. They are tagged `prompt_example` and kept as a control rather than deleted; scripts/check_fixture_contamination.py fails check_all.sh if any untagged fixture is ever quoted in its prompt again.
coach._history: Was 98.7 against a 16-case set that scored 100.0% (80/80). The suite then had only 6 Japanese cases and was measuring the English side plus whatever Japanese had already been fixed. 30 Japanese N5-N3 cases were added on 2026-08-15 and the honest score fell to 63.5%. The floor dropped because the ruler got longer, NOT because the coach got worse — the 16 original cases still score 80/80.
coach._where_the_loss_is: 16 of the 23 new error cases score 0/5, 13 of those by answering 'Perfectly natural!' to a real mistake. Blind classes: を/に and に/で particle choice, transitive/intransitive pairs (つく/つける, 始まる/始める), たい past tense, counters, register. All 12 clean cases score 5/5, so this is pure under-correction, not over-correction.
coach._where_the_appropriateness_loss_is: The 12 situational-violation cases score 26/60 since level-up fit promotion (was 18-19/60). The remaining misses are over-formal-with-a-friend and missing greeting, where the model produces no fit bullet at all — nothing to promote. Historic detail follows. The 12 cases scored 19/60. Same shape as the rest of this suite: under-correction, not over-correction. The 8 appropriate counterexamples score 40/40, the 12 pre-existing clean cases stay 5/5 each, and a side probe re-running those same 12 THROUGH the situation prompt (which the fixtures do not carry, but the CLI always does) scored 60/60 clean twice. The misses are mostly a routing failure rather than blindness: on 'Give me a large coffee.' and 'Where is my prescription?' the model sees the problem and files it under Level up ('more polite and natural in a service context') while Feedback still says 'Perfectly natural!', and the eval scores Feedback only. An explicit prompt rule sending fit problems to Feedback was tried and measured inert — violations 19/60 with it and 19/60 without — so it was not kept.
coach._regression_would_look_like: a drop with the clean cases newly failing — that would be over-correction, a worse failure than the misses this number already reflects

judge._measured: 93.3% (140/150), 30 cases x 5; one run of slack = 0.67 points. Four cases were added on 2026-09-04 covering the path 6cc6db2 created — an English vocab target graded in a Japanese session, which ~1.3 tasks per Japanese session take and which no fixture had covered.
judge._open18_evidence: Those four fixtures were added to decide OPEN-18 cheaply rather than authoring 401 Japanese targets on a hunch. Result: the LLM path handles it. デカフェ (katakana borrowing) 5/5, off-topic お手洗いはどちらですか 5/5 correctly failed, 薬をください for 'prescription' 5/5 correctly failed. The one case that failed, カフェインレスのコーヒー (native equivalent), was NOT a judging failure but the walk-back bug again: the verdict was NO while its own reason said 「decaf」を用いて注文をしました. Fixed by extending the rescue list; now 5/5. So OPEN-18 is NOT required for correctness — the judge credits both katakana and native equivalents and still refuses off-topic answers. It remains a determinism/latency argument only.
judge._regression_would_look_like: 84.6% with 3 false negatives — the OPEN-01 context bug returning
judge._remaining: case 22 is the one false negative, case 5 the accepted false positive

actor._why_84: Investigated 2026-08-31 after the score drifted from a 94-99 history to 87-92. There is no single regression: the failures are ALL has_vocab=False with zero non-empty reasons, they are almost entirely Japanese (English 96-98%, Japanese 80-92% in back-to-back runs of identical code), and the Japanese count swings 4-10 per 50 — so one case flipping moves the headline ~6 points. Attributed over one run of the 10 Japanese cases: 2 no card emitted, 2 fell back to the canned line, 1 dropped by the venue-noun guard (入国検査事務所, correctly — it IS the venue), 1 by the proper-noun guard. Two mechanisms are legitimate cost of rules tightened deliberately: the Japanese script check and the 何か closed-question fix raised Japanese first-attempt rejection 54%->77%, so more turns end on a salvage or fallback path that carries no vocab card, and 22e9092's guard removes junk cards on purpose. The prompt-cache hypothesis was TESTED AND REFUTED: shared cache 89.0% vs cache_key=None 88.0%, Japanese 80% in both. 84.0 sits three points under the lowest of eight observed runs (87/88/88/89/89/90/91/92) rather than one or two, because a floor of 95.0 and then 92.0 were each set from three runs and each was tripped by the next one.
actor._known_scoring_limitation: A card the guards deliberately drop scores identically to a card the model never produced. From the learner's side both mean no vocab tip, so this is defensible, but it means every future vocab-quality improvement LOWERS this number. Read a drop here together with the guard-drop count before calling it a regression.
actor._measured: 90.0 / 85.0 / 89.0 across three runs on 2026-09-05/06 (the OPEN-12 wrong-script branch), which is why the floor stays at 84.0 rather than rising: the lowest of the three sits 1.0 above it, and the English arm — running byte-identical code, since find_wrong_script returns '' on its first line for any non-Japanese language — read 96.0 / 92.0 / 96.0 across those same runs. A 4-point swing on a 50-sample arm that cannot have changed is the suite's own noise, so no floor above 84.0 is defensible on three readings. This closes the 2026-09-05 note that the 90.0 reading needed a second measurement: it has three, and they say the floor is already right. Earlier history: 94.0 / 96.0 / 98.0 / 98.0 / 99.0 per 100 across five runs of the 20-case set, no code change between them beyond the vocab-label fix. A floor of 95.0 was set from the first three runs and a later run scored 94.0, which would have failed check_evals.sh on noise alone — three samples were not enough to see the spread. 92.0 sits two points under the worst observed.
actor._history: Was 90.0 against a 4-case set that scored 100.0% / 95.0% / 100.0% / 100.0% across four runs — 20 samples could not tell flake from defect. Expanded to 20 cases on 2026-08-16 (10 English / 10 Japanese, all places/roles/speakers taken from app/scenarios/data, all six NPC_MOODS covered). The floor went UP, not down: the wider ruler found no new validate() failure class, so the honest number rose once each flaky iteration was worth 1 point instead of 5.
actor._where_the_loss_is: Every failure has the same shape: validate() returned ok and the vocab block failed to reach the learner. Two sub-classes were mislabelled fields the parser rejected ('exourage:', 'encouragement:' instead of 'encourage:') and turns with no vocab block at all. The mislabelled half is FIXED — parse_vocab now accepts encourag* and any short word label — and the remaining failures observed since are all the absent-block kind, which no parser change can recover. Zero failures on sentence count, closed yes/no questions, emoji or residual markup in 300+ samples. Note the suite is too noisy at n=100 to confirm the label fix by score alone; it is pinned by unit tests instead.
actor._what_this_suite_does_not_measure: Language purity. A separate 30-sample probe over the 10 Japanese cases found simplified-Chinese leakage in 7 (23.3%), almost always in the vocab explanation field ('explanation: 书店，专门卖书的地方。'), and this suite scores every one of them as a pass. is_closed_question is also English-only by design, so a Japanese yes/no turn ('列車のチケットが必要ですか。') passes too.
actor._regression_would_look_like: failures whose reason is non-empty — 'Too many sentences', 'Closed yes/no question' or 'Contains residual markup characters'. Those classes are currently at zero, so any of them appearing is a real defect rather than the vocab-block flake this number already reflects

moods._measured: 100.0% (96/96) twice back to back on 2026-08-19 — zero failures and zero fallbacks in 192 samples. 6 moods x 2 languages x 2 conversations x 4 turns. One sample of slack = 1.04 points; the floor sits three samples under the worst observed.
moods._history: Was 94.4 against 18 samples that were all English, all scenario 0, and all the SAME opening turn — evaluate_mood hardcoded language='English', never grew `messages`, and re-sent [{'user':'Hello!'}] on every one of its 3 'turns'. So the old 100.0% described one venue answering one greeting in one language. The suite was rewritten on 2026-08-19 to thread `language` into build_actor_system_prompt, call_actor and validate, to hold a real 4-turn conversation (appending the vocab-stripped actor line and a fixed learner follow-up, mirroring app/cli.py), and to draw 12 scenarios with a seeded unbiased sample shared across both languages. The score did not move; the ruler got 5.3x longer and much wider. Japanese did NOT fail differently from English — both 96/96 across both runs.
moods._what_this_number_actually_measures: The output of call_actor's REPAIR PIPELINE, not the actor model. Now that `language` is threaded through, call_actor retries up to 3x (script-specific retry note included), then salvages, then falls back — so validate() at the eval layer only sees what survived all of that. A side probe of single raw generations with no retry scored English 2/12 (16.7%) and Japanese 4/12 (33.3%) — SUPERSEDED, see the rawactor entry: that probe scored greetings against the wrong sentence budget and skipped the script check, and the real raw rate is ~68%. Every point between those numbers and 100.0% is the retry loop. First-attempt failures were 'Too many sentences (4/5/6)' x9 in English, and in Japanese 'Wrong script' x3 ('还是您需要找书', 'explanation: 依然的意思是...') plus sentence-count and closed-question misses.
moods._known_hole: FALLBACK_ACTOR_LINE ('Let me check that for you. What would you like to do next?') passes validate() in EVERY language, so a turn where the actor gave up entirely scores as a pass. The suite counts these separately and observed 0/192, so nothing is currently inflating the number — but the score would not drop if that changed.
moods._still_unmeasured: OPEN-13. This suite exercises call_actor. The real mid-conversation turn ships through stream_actor, which never calls validate() at all, so the 100.0% describes the checked path only. The mid-conversation turns here confirm the actor's BEHAVIOUR does not degrade with history (turns 1/2/3/4 each 48/48 across both runs), not that the shipped path enforces anything.
moods._regression_would_look_like: any non-empty failure reason at all, or a non-zero fallback count. Both are at zero over 192 samples, so a single one is signal rather than noise — which is also why this floor is tight.

rawactor._observational: NO THRESHOLD ON PURPOSE. This suite is not in check_evals.sh's default list and has no min_score, so running it via check_evals.sh will refuse rather than gate. It is a diagnostic, not a gate — see _why_no_floor.
rawactor._measured: 68.1% (98/144) over three readings of 48 samples on 2026-09-06: 70.8%, 68.8%, 64.6%. scripts/eval_rawactor.py --seed 42. 12 seeded scenarios x 2 languages x {greeting, mid-conversation}, moods cycled over all six NPC_MOODS, one generation each scored by validate() with no retry, salvage or fallback.
rawactor._why_no_floor: The spread is too wide to gate and the reason is arithmetic, not tuning. At n=48 and p~0.68 the binomial standard error is 6.7 points, so a 95% interval is +/-13. Observed spreads match: total 64.6-70.8 (6.2), English 75.0-87.5 (12.5), Japanese 41.7-66.7 (25.0), and the Japanese greeting cell swung 75.0/75.0/25.0 across three readings of identical code. Any floor loose enough not to fire on that noise would sit near 55% and would not catch a real regression. Tightening to a +/-2 point interval needs about 544 samples per reading, roughly 70 minutes at the measured 7.7s/sample, which is far outside what a gate can cost. Read this number as a level, never as a pass/fail, and compare medians of several readings rather than single runs.
rawactor._what_it_is_for: The repaired suites (actor 90%, moods 100%) call call_actor, which retries 3x then salvages then falls back, so they cannot see the actor regress until repair stops covering for it — and repair is the part that keeps changing. This scores the first generation, and its REASON DISTRIBUTION is the real output: over 144 samples, 27x Closed yes/no question, 11x Too many sentences, 8x Wrong script. Those say which rule the actor trips, which no repaired score can. The closed-question count in particular is invisible downstream because salvage_actor_output strips exactly those sentences.
rawactor._supersedes: The 16.7-33.3% raw figures previously quoted in BACKLOG.md (OPEN-14) and in the moods entry below came from scratch/measure_greeting.py and are MEASURED WRONG, in both directions at once. That probe scored greetings against max_sentences=3 when GREETING_MAX_SENTENCES is 4, so compliant 4-sentence greetings counted as failures and the number is biased low — and 'Too many sentences' was its dominant failure class, which is what that bug manufactures. It also passed no language, so find_wrong_script never ran and every Japanese script leak scored as a pass, biasing Japanese high. It also used mood='neutral', which is not one of the six NPC_MOODS, so it measured a prompt the app never sends. The real raw rate is ~68%, not ~25%: the repair pipeline contributes roughly 20 points, not 60.
rawactor._regression_would_look_like: a sustained shift in the reason mix across several readings — Wrong script climbing would mean the script denylist has a hole, Too many sentences climbing would mean the sentence rule has stopped binding. A single reading moving 10 points means nothing at this sample size.
